tldr: This paper introduces HEIR, a large-scale HRI dataset that synchronizes human speech, gaze, and egocentric video with mobile bimanual robot action logs, providing an end-to-end evaluation from human intent understanding to navigation and manipulation planning and execution. While human gaze and viewpoint dramatically improve intent understanding accuracy, the end-to-end task success rate on the real robot reached only 18.52%, highlighting error accumulation across modules as a major bottleneck for practical deployment.
hero_caption: An example of a long-horizon HRI session in HEIR. It begins with natural spoken instructions grounded in the user's egocentric viewpoint and gaze, which unfold into sequential navigation and manipulation subtasks based on disambiguated task specifications. The top-down view on the right illustrates the robot's spatial movements and environmental state changes across multiple episodes.
overview:
In recent years, Embodied AI has progressed rapidly with the emergence of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and robot foundation models. However, most of these remain within a robot-centric paradigm where the robot simply carries out pre-specified instructions, often treating humans merely as obstacles or external factors. To realize robots that can genuinely collaborate with and assist humans in the real world, a "human-centric" approach that places human intent and behavior at the core of task formulation is essential.

To address this, the authors introduce HEIR, a dataset designed to study long-horizon human-robot interaction (HRI) in natural home environments. HEIR synchronizes human gaze measured via eye-tracking glasses, egocentric video, and speech with the navigation and manipulation trajectory logs of a mobile bimanual robot down to the millisecond. It contains numerous natural interactions involving demonstrative pronouns like "bring me that" and scenarios where the referenced object is visible only from the human's perspective, not the robot's.

Using this dataset, the authors designed a four-tier evaluation benchmark consisting of "Intent Understanding," "Subtask Planning," "Navigation (VLN)," and "Manipulation (VLA/WAM)," conducting both offline and real-robot evaluations.

The results demonstrated that combining human gaze with an egocentric viewpoint dramatically boosts intent understanding accuracy. However, in an integrated end-to-end evaluation on the physical robot, even when individual subtask success rates were relatively high, the overall episode success rate remained at only 18.52%. This highlights the severe compounding of errors in long-horizon tasks and points out clear future challenges for human-centric robotics.
contributions: Released a real-world HRI dataset (38.56 hours, 1,836 episodes) that completely synchronizes human egocentric video, high-precision gaze data, and speech with mobile bimanual robot observations and teleoperation trajectories.
Established an integrated evaluation benchmark spanning four hierarchical tiers: Intent Understanding, Subtask Planning, Navigation, and Manipulation.
Quantitatively demonstrated that human gaze information, egocentric viewpoints, and past interaction history substantially improve intent understanding accuracy for ambiguous instructions.
Built a closed-loop control system on a physical robot integrating state-of-the-art VLA and VLN models, uncovering the critical challenge of error accumulation in long-horizon interactions.

sections.heading: Shifting from Robot-Centric to Human-Centric Embodied AI
sections.summary: Conventional robot learning has focused heavily on task execution from the robot's viewpoint while neglecting human context. This section discusses the background behind why a new dataset like HEIR—incorporating human gaze and egocentric perspectives—is needed to achieve human-centric decision making.
sections.details:
Riding on the success of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), robotics has seen surging interest in VLA models that directly bind vision, language, and action, as well as action generation based on World Action Models (WAM). Furthermore, systems capable of handling long-horizon tasks by chaining multiple modules using LLM agent techniques have begun to appear.

However, the vast majority of these advances remain "task-centric." In other words, they focus entirely on executing clear, given instructions, treating humans merely as "obstacles to avoid." Yet, when considering assistive robots in real homes, humans are not outside the task; they are the central actors who dynamically alter task goals in real time through their actions, gaze, and speech.

To solve this challenge, data capturing not just the robot's own sensor streams, but also "how humans perceive the world and how they communicate with the robot" is indispensable. Prior HRI datasets have been skewed toward short tabletop tasks, lacking any comprehensive resource that captures long-horizon tasks mixing navigation with manipulation alongside human egocentric video and gaze data.

Therefore, this study introduces HEIR, simultaneously recording human egocentric video, measured gaze, speech, and the robot's bimanual manipulation and mobile base trajectories. By linking human context directly to robot behavior, it aims to lay the groundwork for genuinely human-aligned robot intelligence.

sections.heading: Limitations of Existing Datasets and What Sets HEIR Apart
sections.summary: Reviewing existing robot action datasets and HRI benchmarks clarifies what was missing. HEIR is the only real-world dataset that brings together paired human-robot perspectives, gaze, speech, long-horizon tasks, navigation, and bimanual manipulation in a single package.
sections.details:
With the advent of large-scale robotic datasets, standalone robot manipulation skills have advanced dramatically. However, resources that can handle natural interactions with humans remain extremely scarce.

Prior works include HABIT, which explores human-robot collaborative actions and gestures; HARMONIC, which records gaze during feeding assistance; and HandMeThat, which attempts context understanding under ambiguous instructions. Additionally, studies like WatchAct have investigated deriving robot execution plans from human egocentric action videos.

Nonetheless, previous research suffered from notable constraints: short tabletop tasks, simulated environments, or fixed camera viewpoints. In the real world, interactions where navigation and bimanual manipulation seamlessly intertwine—such as tidying up a room or handing over objects while moving across rooms—have barely been explored.

HEIR's outstanding strength lies in bringing together human egocentric video, eye-tracked gaze, spoken audio, the robot's own multi-camera streams, and teleoperated mobile and manipulation trajectories. No prior work has integrated all of these elements into a single real-world dataset.

sections.heading: Capturing Human Gaze and Robot Actions: Collection and Annotation Protocol
sections.summary: Using eye-tracking glasses and a mobile bimanual robot, 38.56 hours of household collaborative interaction data were gathered. Precise time synchronization between human and robot was performed, and hierarchical task structures with dense subtask goal annotations were generated using VLMs.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Task Formulation and Hierarchical Interaction Structure
In HEIR, household interactions are organized into a three-tier hierarchy: sessions, episodes, and subtasks. A single session averages 7.71 minutes and contains multiple consecutive episodes (6.12 on average). Each episode starts with a single spoken command from the human (e.g., "Bring me that"), which unfolds into an average of 3.49 sequential navigation and manipulation subtasks to achieve it. A key feature is physical environment continuity, where an object moved in an earlier episode can become the target of a subsequent instruction.

### 3.2 Multimodal Data Collection Setup
Participants (17 in total) wore Pupil Labs Neon eye-tracking glasses, giving instructions to the robot using natural speech and gaze. The robot platform was a Galaxea R1 Lite mobile bimanual robot, logging stereo head cameras, dual wrist cameras, and state trajectories for its arms, grippers, torso lift, and mobile base. An expert operator in a separate room observed a global camera view to teleoperate the robot, executing handovers and transports in real time.

Synchronizing camera streams required special care. Stopwatches were filmed by both human and robot cameras at the start and end of each recording. Using linear interpolation, the clock drift of approximately 4 seconds over 10 minutes (0.67%) was corrected. Audio was time-stretched while preserving pitch, and gaze coordinates were aligned frame-by-frame.

### 3.3 Human and VLM-Assisted Annotation
Annotation proceeded in two stages. First, human annotators inspected speech, gaze, and egocentric video to strictly label referenced target objects, target locations, nominal plans, and subtask boundaries. Next, leveraging GPT-5.6, specific subgoals (what needs to be done) and completion conditions (what constitutes completion) were verbalized in detail for each subtask. All annotations underwent rigorous final human inspection.

### 3.4 & 3.5 Geometric Validation of Base Trajectories and Dataset Statistics
Mobile base trajectories were reconstructed by fusing wheel odometry with the visual odometry method MapAnything, aligned to the spatial frame of a MID-360 LiDAR scan. Verification against ground-truth measurements from an external HTC VIVE tracker confirmed high precision, achieving a position RMSE of 8.55 cm and a cosine similarity of 0.9992 for local movement directions.
The complete dataset spans 20 daily task categories (housekeeping, kitchen, study tasks, etc.), 300 sessions, 1,836 episodes, and 6,416 subtasks, totaling 38.56 hours of recorded time.

sections.heading: Four Benchmarks from Intent Understanding to Physical Execution
sections.summary: To benchmark the value of HEIR, four hierarchical evaluation tasks were established. Clear evaluation metrics are defined across each stage: Human Intent Understanding, Subtask Planning, Vision-Language Navigation, and Bimanual Manipulation.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Human Intent Understanding
Taking spoken speech, egocentric video with gaze, robot observations, and past dialogue history as input, this task predicts the target object, target location, and intended execution phases before the robot begins moving. Following standard dialogue tasks, evaluation relies on Slot micro-F1 for extracted slots, Location Accuracy (Location Acc) for target locations, Robot View Visibility F1 (RV F1), and Plan Exact Match (Plan EM) for the planned sequence of phases.

### 4.2 Subtask Planning
This task manages closed-loop execution based on inferred human intent and current robot states. At each decision point, the planner outputs a 3-way classification: "Continue" (keep running current subtask), "Switch" (transition to the next subtask, outputting new subgoals and completion conditions), or "Done" (episode completed). This measures whether the planner can adaptively transition based on environmental changes.

### 4.3 Navigation
Given a navigation subgoal (e.g., "move to the white cabinet"), robot foundation models or VLN models generate mobile base control commands (forward, turn left, turn right, stop). In addition to single-step action accuracy and F1 scores, the benchmark emphasizes "Stop F1," which assesses whether the robot stops cleanly at the goal.

### 4.4 Manipulation
Following a manipulation subgoal (e.g., "pick up the blue folder with the right arm"), VLA models or WAMs generate trajectories for the arms and grippers. Models are evaluated using Joint space Mean Squared Error (Joint MSE), end-effector position error (cm), and rotation error (degrees) for both the 1-step prediction and a 24-step chunk prediction.

### 4.5 Real-Robot End-to-End Evaluation
By integrating all four modules into a unified system, this benchmark evaluates whether the robot can fulfill natural human requests from start to finish in physical environments without human intervention.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Gaze Brings Dramatic Gains, but Physical Integration Hits a Wall
sections.summary: Human gaze and egocentric viewpoints significantly boost intent understanding, while fine-tuning substantially enhances planning, navigation, and manipulation. However, when chaining these together on a real robot, cascading errors kept the long-horizon task completion rate at just 18.52%.
sections.details:
### 5.1 The Impact of Multimodality on Human Intent Understanding
Experiments using Gemma-4-31B and other base models revealed key insights. Using speech text alone (Instruction only), the Slot F1 was limited to 59.60%. Adding robot-view video boosted it to 76.71%. Incorporating human egocentric video raised it to 81.02%, and overlaying measured gaze pushed it to 82.46% (with target location accuracy reaching 84.51%). Actual measured gaze clearly outperformed a simple center-of-screen heuristic (Center prior), proving that knowing what the human is looking at plays a decisive role in resolving ambiguities. Providing past episode history further improved intent understanding accuracy.

### 5.2 Planner Fine-Tuning
Pre-trained VLM planners (such as Cosmos3-Nano and Qwen3.5-4B) failed to assess subtask progress from images zero-shot, tending to output "Continue" almost every time. However, fine-tuning on HEIR produced a sharp jump in decision accuracy by 25 to 37 percentage points. In particular, Qwen3.5-4B achieved a 61.06% Core accuracy in predicting new subtask content during transitions.

### 5.3 & 5.4 Navigation and Manipulation: Offline vs. Real-Robot Comparison
Navigation models (like InternVLA-N1) and manipulation models (such as Lingbot-VLA2, FastWAM, and $\pi_{0.5}$) also saw their prediction errors substantially reduced through adaptation training on HEIR. In real-robot pick-and-place tests (20 tasks $\times$ 3 trials each), Lingbot-VLA2 achieved a 68.33% success rate, FastWAM achieved 60.00%, and $\pi_{0.5}$ reached 36.67%. These results matched the offline trajectory error rankings cleanly, confirming that offline metrics serve as strong indicators of real-world performance.

### 5.5 Long-Horizon Evaluation on the Integrated Real-Robot System
Combining the strongest modules, the authors ran an end-to-end evaluation on the physical robot across 27 episodes. While the standalone navigation subtask success rate was high at 81.25%, the overall episode success rate chaining intent understanding, planning, navigation, and manipulation plummeted to just 18.52%. A slight perceptual misalignment would induce a planner misjudgment, cascading into manipulation failures—sharply highlighting the severity of compounding errors in long-horizon tasks.

sections.heading: A New Milestone for Human-Centric Robotics
sections.summary: HEIR is a pioneering dataset bridging human egocentric intent expressions with embodied robot actions. Benchmark experiments demonstrate the immense utility of leveraging human intent, while underscoring the uncharted challenge of integrating long-horizon tasks in real-world settings.
sections.details:
This study established HEIR, a dataset and integrated benchmark designed to enable long-horizon human-robot collaboration in household settings. Demonstrating the powerful signal provided by human gaze and egocentric video for instruction grounding offers a vital guidepost for future Embodied AI and HRI research.

At the same time, the sharp drop in success rate when chaining capable individual modules together on a physical robot highlights a fundamental challenge the robotics community must tackle. The data and hierarchical evaluation framework provided by HEIR offer a sturdy foundation toward realizing truly human-centric, autonomous collaborative robots.

sections.heading: Appendix: Real-Robot Integration Pipeline and Implementation Details
sections.summary: Details on the event-driven hierarchical software pipeline supporting real-robot deployment, along with model training hyperparameters and synchronization methods, are outlined here.
sections.details:
### Hierarchical Pipeline for Real-Robot Control
In the physical deployment, the system continuously listens for audio. When speech is detected, the intent reasoner (Qwen3.8-27B) triggers immediately. The reasoner rapidly infers structured intent from past intent history, current egocentric gaze video, and robot cameras. This model is optimized for lightweight, low-latency inference.

Upon receiving its output, the closed-loop planner (Qwen3.5-4B) is invoked event-driven rather than at a fixed rate, triggering when the robot enters an idle state ($\tau_{\text{idle}} = 20$ seconds of no action). This prevents plans from interrupting active navigation or arm motions prematurely, ensuring safe and stable subtask execution.

### Training and Evaluation Setup Details
For navigation model training, LoRA (rank 32, alpha 64) was used, adapting only the language decoder's attention and FFN layers. Accurately learning when to stop (STOP) is particularly critical. Stationary periods within 2 cm of the target, within 3 degrees of target orientation, and with wheel speed below 0.01 m/s were strictly labeled as STOP ground truth. An auxiliary STOP loss term (weight coefficient 0.25) was introduced to prevent overshooting.

captions.F5: Overall hierarchical execution pipeline on the real robot. Triggered by a user's spoken command, the intent reasoner identifies the target object ("blue folder"), target location ("speaker"), and nominal plan using egocentric gaze video and robot cameras, after which the closed-loop planner dispatches tasks to the navigation and manipulation backends.

takeaways: Gaze is the ultimate prompt: Even with ambiguous speech and demonstrative pronouns, overlaying human gaze information onto egocentric views dramatically improves robot intent understanding and object localization.

Don't rely on zero-shot planners: Out of the box, state-of-the-art VLMs almost always fail to recognize task completion from robot observations, making domain-specific fine-tuning for action transitions essential.

Offline error is an excellent proxy for real-world performance: Rankings of offline trajectory prediction errors (Joint MSE, position error) for VLAs and WAMs align closely with physical pick-and-place success rates.

Sum of subtask successes $\neq$ long-horizon success: Even if individual modules achieve 60–80% success, error compounding drops end-to-end real-robot completion to under 20%, highlighting the urgent need for retry and recovery mechanisms.
limitations: The experimental setup is confined to a single laboratory environment (with rearranged furniture in the same room), leaving zero-shot generalization to unseen house layouts untested.
The real-robot setup lacks an autonomous recovery or retry mechanism when a subtask fails, meaning a single mistake immediately leads to failure of the entire episode.

The system assumes the user constantly wears eye-tracking glasses, posing a practical hardware hurdle for how to acquire equivalent gaze and egocentric information from unencumbered users in daily homes.
